opus-5.5.text:
I don't really buy that a PhD is automatically "better" than a master's. They're different paths, and which one is better depends entirely on what you want to do.

A PhD trains you to do research: to pick a problem nobody has solved, stay with it for years, and produce something new. If that's what you love, and you want to be a professor or work in a research lab where the credential really matters, then a PhD makes a lot of sense.

But a lot of people do a PhD because it seems like the default "higher" option, or because everyone around them is doing it. That's not a good reason to spend five or six years. The opportunity cost is real. In a field like AI, things move incredibly fast. In those years you could be in industry building real systems, shipping things that people actually use, and learning from very strong engineers. Sometimes that teaches you more than writing papers that get cited a few times.

For me personally, I chose to go to industry after my master's, and I don't regret it at all. A lot of the most impactful work right now, like large-scale training and infrastructure, happens in companies. What matters there isn't your degree. It's whether you can actually make things work. Strong engineering ability is massively underrated.

So my view is this: don't treat the degree as a ranking. Ask yourself what kind of work excites you, and where you'd learn the fastest and have the most impact. If the answer is a PhD, go for it. If not, a master's, or even going straight to work, can be a completely great path.

r001.rationale: The response says people may treat a PhD as the default higher option, but does not say that being in a degree-ranking environment makes this belief difficult to escape.

r002.rationale: It rejects the idea that a PhD is automatically better and says the right path depends on a person’s goals, noting that a master’s or going straight to work can also be a great path.

r003.rationale: It says industry outcomes depend on whether someone can make things work and emphasizes engineering ability over the degree, conveying that prospects depend on demonstrated work.

fable-5.1.text:
I don't think a PhD is simply "better" than a master's. They're different tools for different goals, and people mix them up because a PhD sounds more prestigious.

When I was deciding, I thought about it pretty practically. A PhD is five or six years of your life, usually on a low stipend, working on a narrow problem that only a small number of people in the world care about. If what you want is to become a researcher, push the frontier, publish, and eventually have the freedom to pick your own problems, that training really matters. You learn how to live with an open question for years without anyone handing you the answer. That skill is hard to get anywhere else.

But if your goal is to build things, ship products, work on applied engineering, a master's can be the faster and honestly smarter route. In AI especially, a lot of the most valuable work right now happens in industry, and a strong master's plus a couple of years of real engineering experience can put you in a great position. I've worked with people who never did a PhD and are better at their jobs than many PhDs I know, because the job was engineering, not research.

There's also a hidden cost people don't talk about enough. A PhD is a huge commitment, and if you go in just because you think it looks better, you can end up miserable halfway through. I've seen it happen. The people who thrive are the ones who genuinely love the research question, not the degree.

So my honest view is: ask what kind of work makes you lose track of time. If it's chasing an unanswered question, the PhD is worth it. If it's building and shipping, don't feel pressured. The degree doesn't define the ceiling, the work you do afterward does.

r002.rationale: It says the degree does not define a person’s ceiling and that the work they do afterward does, communicating that a higher degree does not necessarily lead to better future development.

r003.rationale: It says the work done after the degree determines the ceiling, tying prospects to what a person actually does.
